sermon:
A young pastor stands in a city famous for its temple, its commerce, and its talkers. Ephesus did not lack religion. It lacked the gospel. And Paul, somewhere on a hard road, writes back to the man he left in charge with a single sentence that doubles as a command: "As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine" (1 Timothy 1:3). The first word to a young minister is not encouragement. It is a charge. Stay, and silence the men who are turning the faith into a hobby for the clever.

**The Law Was Never a Sandbox**

The teachers in Ephesus had discovered something intoxicating. They could take the law of God and turn it into endless genealogies, speculations, myths, a game with no bottom and no cost. They wanted to be teachers of the law without the faintest idea what the law was for. Paul will not allow it. The law, he says, is good if one uses it lawfully, and its lawful use is brutal. It exists to expose. It is laid down for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the people who do not think they need it. The law is not material for a seminar. It is a diagnosis. It names what is wrong in you, and it was never given to flatter the religious.

This is the quiet danger in every church with smart people in it. We can spend a lifetime discussing the things of God and never once let those things land on us. We can master the text and miss the verdict. The Ephesian teachers were not immoral in any way that would make the newspapers. They were worse. They had made God's word a means of feeling important, and the moment Scripture stops accusing you, it has become an idol you control.

**The Worst Man in the Room Wrote This Letter**

Then Paul does the thing that disarms every speculator. He turns the law on himself. The man writing the charge was, by his own testimony, a blasphemer, a persecutor, an insolent opponent. He held the coats while Stephen died. And he says it plainly: "The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). Not was. Am. He does not graduate out of the category. He stays inside the indictment, and that is why he can be trusted to charge another man.

Why did mercy find him. Paul gives the reason without flinching: so that in him, the worst of them, Christ Jesus might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe. Paul is not the hero of his own rescue. He is the evidence. If grace reached him, the genealogy-spinners had no excuse, and neither do we. The point of his sin is not his shame. It is Christ's patience.

**The Charge We Cannot Soften**

Here is where the law and the gospel meet, and where every preacher must decide what he is for. The law exposes the lawless and drives them to the only one who can save them. Strip the law of its severity and you also empty the cross of its necessity. The Ephesian teachers wanted theology without the wound. Paul wants the wound, because only the wounded come to the physician.

I cannot preach this letter from above it. I am not the doctor in this scene. I am another man whom mercy reached, charged now to say hard things to other sinners because someone once said hard things to me. We did not earn the silence Paul commands; we received it. And the gospel that saved the foremost is the only gospel strong enough to silence the clever and raise the dead.

To the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever. That is how Paul ends the section. Not with strategy. With worship.

Mercy found the worst of us.

Ask a church what it does first, and watch the answers come: we teach, we serve, we gather, we sing. Paul, ordering the worship of a young congregation under pressure, puts something else at the front of the line. "First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people" (1 Timothy 2:1). First of all. Before the sermon, before the offering, before the strategy meeting, the church on its knees for people it will never meet.

**Pray for All, Because God Wills All**

Paul does not leave the command floating. He grounds it in the heart of God. We pray for kings and all who are in high positions, for everyone, because God our Savior desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The reason the church prays widely is that God loves widely. A congregation that prays only for itself has shrunk its God to the size of its own membership roll.

This cuts against the instinct of a beleaguered church. Ephesus was small and the empire was vast and the temptation was to pray defensively, for survival, for our people, for our walls. Paul refuses the small prayer. He sends them out past their own doors, to pray for the very officials who could persecute them, so that the church might lead a peaceful and quiet life, not for comfort, but for the spread of the truth. Intercession is the first act of a church that believes the gospel is for the world and not for the club.

**One God, One Mediator, One Ransom**

Then comes the engine underneath it all. Why pray for all. Because there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. There are not many roads and we pray for travelers on each. There is one bridge across the chasm, and we pray that people will be carried over it. The exclusivity of Christ does not narrow our prayers. It widens them. Precisely because he is the only mediator, we must intercede for everyone, since no one is reached by any other name.

Hear the cost folded into the word ransom. A ransom is paid when someone is held captive and cannot free himself. Paul testified in the previous chapter that he was the foremost of sinners; here he tells us how the foremost was bought back. Christ gave himself. The mediator did not negotiate from a safe distance. He stepped into the chasm and became the bridge with his own body. We pray for all people because one man died for all people, and the testimony was given at the proper time.

**Worship That Adorns Instead of Distracts**

The rest of the chapter, often handled clumsily, follows from this. If worship is ordered around prayer for all people, then everything in the gathering must adorn the gospel rather than compete with it. The men are to pray without anger and quarreling, because a church at war with itself cannot intercede for the world. The women are to adorn themselves with good works rather than with display, because the gathering is not a place to be seen but a place to plead for those who are perishing. The whole instruction is about removing distractions so the church can do its first work: lifting holy hands for a world that does not yet know its Savior.

I confess I find this order hard. My prayers default inward, to my burdens, my church, my name. Paul indicts that reflex and sends me outward to the very people I would rather ignore. The church that prays only for itself has forgotten that it was once outside, prayed for by someone, ransomed by one.

There is one mediator. Everything else in the room is arrangement. The center is a man who gave himself, and the first thing we do in his name is plead for the people he died to save.

One mediator. Pray for all.

We have a way of choosing leaders. We look for the gifted, the magnetic, the man who fills a room and a calendar. Paul, writing to a church that will outlive its founders, looks somewhere else entirely. He sets down the qualifications for those who would oversee the household of God, and the striking thing is what is missing. Almost nothing on the list is a skill. Nearly everything is a character. The office, in Paul's hands, requires the man before it requires the talent.

**Above Reproach Is Not a Suggestion**

Read the catalog of an overseer and feel its weight. He must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. Only one item, able to teach, touches competence. The rest is the slow accumulation of a life. You cannot cram for this. You cannot fake it for a season. It is who a man has become when no one was assigning him a platform.

And then Paul reaches for the home: "He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?" (1 Timothy 3:4-5). The household is the proving ground. Not the conference stage, not the sermon, the kitchen table. A man's family knows whether his godliness is real, because they have seen him tired, angry, cornered, and small. Paul makes the private room the test of public fitness. He must also be well thought of by outsiders, by the people with no reason to flatter him.

The deacons follow the same logic. Tested first, then let them serve. Holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. A clear conscience is not the absence of failure. It is the presence of repentance, a man who keeps short accounts with God and owes no hidden debt to sin.

**The House They Are Guarding**

Why does the standard run so high. Because of what the church is. Paul names it without decoration: the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth. This is not a club that survives mediocre management. It is the structure that holds the truth up before a watching world. A pillar that is corrupt at the base brings down everything resting on it. The leaders must embody what they guard, or the truth they hold sags in the eyes of everyone outside.

This is why character cannot be optional. A gifted teacher with a rotten conscience is not a strong pillar with a flaw. He is a fault line. The church does not need impressive men. It needs trustworthy ones, because the building bears weight.

**The Mystery the Office Serves**

Then Paul ends the chapter by telling us what the pillar holds up. He breaks into what sounds like an early hymn: great indeed is the mystery of godliness, he was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory. Christ himself is the godliness the leaders are charged to embody. The character on the list is not generic decency. It is the shape of the one who came in the flesh and gave himself.

I will not pretend to read this list comfortably. Every man who leads in the church reads it and feels the gap. I feel it. The office I hold does not measure my gifts; it measures my life, and my life is a work God is still doing. The honest response is not despair and not pretense, but the long, unglamorous labor of becoming the kind of man the office requires, kept by the grace of the one who was manifested in the flesh.

We wanted to know who should lead. Paul answers by describing not a resume but a man.

The office requires the man.

Some errors arrive wearing the robes of holiness. The teachers troubling Ephesus were not libertines. They were stricter than the apostles. They forbade marriage and required abstinence from foods, and they wore their prohibitions like medals. Paul names this for what it is, a doctrine of demons dressed as devotion, and against it he sets a single discipline for the minister: train yourself for godliness. The answer to false severity is not laxity. It is a deeper kind of work.

**Everything God Made, Received With Thanks**

Paul will not let the ascetics own the high ground. He answers their prohibitions with the doctrine of creation: everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer. The world is not a trap to escape. It is a gift to receive rightly. The forbidding of good things looks spiritual and is actually a slander against the Maker, who called his creation good and never revoked the verdict.

So the good minister is fed differently than the false teacher. He is not nourished on rules and rumors and the latest controversy. He is being trained, Paul says, in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that he has followed. What goes into a minister determines what comes out. A man marinating in speculation will dispense speculation. A man fed on sound teaching has something to give.

**Train, Because Godliness Is Earned Like Strength**

Then the central command, and it is athletic: "for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come" (1 Timothy 4:8). Train. The word is the one from the gymnasium, sweat and repetition and the long obedience of a body being shaped. Paul does not say godliness will descend on you if you wait. He says it must be trained for, the way a runner trains, with discipline that hurts before it helps and shows no results for a long while.

This rebukes the way I want holiness, which is suddenly and without cost. I want to be godly the way the Ephesians wanted to be spiritual, through a rule I can keep and feel superior about. Paul offers something slower and far more demanding: the daily, unglamorous repetition of prayer, Scripture, and obedience, practiced when no one watches and nothing feels different. There is no shortcut. There is only training.

And the stakes are not private. Paul tells the young man to let no one despise his youth, but to set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. The minister's life is the example before it is the lesson. People will believe the gospel they see embodied before they believe the gospel they merely hear.

**Keep Watch, and Be Kept**

Paul gathers it into a charge that has steadied ministers for two thousand years: keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers. Notice the order. Yourself first. A man can preach truth and lose his own soul if he watches the doctrine and never watches the man teaching it. The two must be guarded together, the life and the teaching, because a hearer is helped by neither alone.

Where is Christ in this labor. He is the toil itself. Paul says we labor and strive because we have our hope set on the living God, the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe. We do not train to earn a salvation we lack. We train because we are already kept by a Savior, and the discipline is how that grace works itself into the muscle of an actual life.

The false teachers offered a holiness you could wear. Paul offers one you must become, watched closely, day after day, in the strength of the God who saves.

Train yourself. Watch your life.

A church will tell you what it believes by how it treats its weakest members when no one important is looking. Paul, ordering relationships in Ephesus, refuses to leave honor and justice to instinct. He walks through the household of God room by room, the old and the young, the widows, the elders, and he insists that grace must take concrete, sometimes expensive, shape. The church is a family, and families are tested at the edges, where the vulnerable are and where the money is.

**Family Before Charity**

Paul begins with how to speak. Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. The church is to talk to itself the way a healthy family talks, with honor running in every direction. This is not sentiment. It is the structure underneath everything that follows.

Then the hard, specific case of the widows. Paul will not let compassion become carelessness. The church must honor widows who are truly widows, alone and dependent, but families must first care for their own. He puts it bluntly: "But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). The church's charity is not meant to excuse a family from its duty. Real love is discriminating; it directs help where it is genuinely needed and presses responsibility back onto those who should carry it. Compassion without justice merely subsidizes neglect.

**Honor the Elders, Judge No One Rashly**

Paul turns to the leaders and the same balance holds, honor joined to justice. Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. The church owes its faithful leaders real support, including material support; Paul quotes the principle that the laborer deserves his wages. A congregation that lets its faithful ministers go hungry has misunderstood honor.

But honor does not mean immunity. In the same breath Paul protects elders from slander and holds them accountable: do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses, yet those who persist in sin are to be rebuked in the presence of all. No witch hunts and no cover-ups. The same justice that shields a man from gossip exposes him when sin is proven. And Paul charges Timothy to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality. The church is to be a place where the powerful are not above correction and the accused are not below protection.

I find both walls inconvenient, which is how I know they are needed. I would rather believe the charge against a man I dislike and dismiss the one against a man I admire. Paul forbids both. Justice in the household of God does not bend to my affections.

**The Family the Cross Made**

Why order the church this way, with such care for widows and such evenhandedness toward elders. Because of what made the church a family in the first place. We are not relatives by blood. We are relatives by the cross, brought into one household by the one who had nowhere to lay his head, who saw the widow at the treasury and the poor at the gate. The church treats its weakest with honor because its Lord did, and because every one of us was once the weak member someone was commanded to honor.

This chapter ends with a quiet realism that I need. Paul says the sins of some are conspicuous and others appear later, and the good works of some are conspicuous and others cannot remain hidden. We do not always see clearly who is faithful and who is fraud. So we act with honor and justice now, and we trust the final reckoning to the one who sees what we cannot.

A church is known by how it loves the ones who can do nothing for it.

Honor the church as family.

There is a religion that pays, and it always finds a market. The teachers Paul confronts at the close of this letter had figured out that godliness could be turned into a revenue stream, that piety dressed up well could open wallets. Paul names the error and then opens his hand to show the antidote, which is not poverty but contentment, a settled freedom from the hunger that drives men to use God for gain.

**Contentment Is the Great Gain**

Paul does not deny that godliness brings gain. He redefines the gain. Godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world and we cannot take anything out of it. We arrived with empty hands and we leave the same way, and somewhere in between we convince ourselves the accumulation matters eternally. If we have food and clothing, Paul says, with these we will be content. The whole anxious project of more is exposed as a forgetting of how we came and how we go.

Then the famous warning, so often misquoted that we should hear it exactly: "For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs" (1 Timothy 6:10). Not money, the love of it. And notice who does the piercing. They pierced themselves. Greed is not a wound inflicted from outside. It is self-inflicted, a slow impaling that the greedy man performs on his own soul while telling himself he is only being prudent.

**A Word to Those Who Have It**

Paul does not pretend the rich do not exist in the church, nor does he simply condemn them. He charges them. As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. The command to the wealthy is not to feel guilty but to be generous, to do good, to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up treasure for the future. Money is not the enemy. The hope set on money is the enemy. The cure is an open hand.

I cannot preach this as a man standing outside its reach. I live in the most prosperous corner of human history, and the love of money is the air I breathe without noticing. The teachers who imagined godliness was a means of gain are not a distant heresy; they are a temptation that visits every minister who has ever eyed a larger platform and a larger income and called the ambition a calling. We did this. The contentment Paul commands is not native to me. It must be learned, against the grain, in the presence of the God who is himself enough.

**Flee, Pursue, Fight**

So Paul ends the letter with three verbs hurled at his young pastor. Flee these things. Run from the love of money the way you run from fire. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. And fight the good fight of the faith, take hold of the eternal life to which you were called. The Christian life is not a stroll. It is a flight, a pursuit, and a war, all at once.

And underneath it all, the deposit. Paul's final charge: guard the good deposit entrusted to you. The faith is not Timothy's to edit or to sell. It is a treasure handed to him to protect and pass on intact. Where is Christ in this. He is the one who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, who though rich became poor, who fought his own good fight to the cross so that men enslaved to gain could be set free. We fight because he fought first, and we flee greed because we have found something richer.

The teachers wanted godliness to pay. Paul wanted godliness, full stop, and a man willing to war for it.

Flee greed. Fight for faith.
